claims.text: The target material is a nearly defect-free, low-oxygen HfNbTaTiZr alloy.
Arc melting followed by homogenization can validate or produce the claimed low-oxygen, nearly defect-free state.
A phonon Boltzmann transport calculation using DFT-derived anharmonic force constants can separately predict lattice thermal transport.
KKR-CPA relaxation times with higher-order corrections can separately predict electronic thermal transport.
Benchmarking the electronic model against mobility data will refine its relaxation times.
The proposed model is applicable over 100–1200 K for low-oxygen HfNbTaTiZr.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
High-temperature measurements of HfNbTaTiZr give total thermal conductivities of 10–17 W/(K m).
Chemical complexity produces disordered electronic band structures in the alloy.
Chemical and structural fluctuations affect lattice vibrations and phonon scattering in compositionally complex materials.
Independent calculation of phonon lifetimes and electronic scattering rates separates the lattice and electronic heat-transport channels.
The separated calculations will identify a heat-carrier crossover near 200 K.
Electronic heat conduction dominates below approximately 200 K, while phonon conduction dominates above the crossover and above room temperature.
The proposed approach will improve predictive accuracy by approximately 15–20% relative to global-Debye models.
Predicted high-temperature total thermal conductivities will fall within 10–17 W/(K m).
Existing analytical models rely on a single Debye-temperature approximation and perfect-crystal assumptions that conflate lattice and electronic scattering.
The method will be less reliable for oxygen-contaminated or defect-rich HfNbTaTiZr because those defects are not represented in the model.
Electronic relaxation times in chemically disordered systems remain uncertain and require calibration against mobility or scattering measurements.

contradictions.description: The 10–17 W/(K m) high-temperature benchmark is applied to low-oxygen, nearly defect-free samples even though the task identifies that benchmark as coming from a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen, while the boundary states that oxygen contamination reduces applicability.
